content: The study by Takito et al. (2010), which included 272 cases and 546 controls, found no association between prenatal exercise and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Similarly, Cavalcante et al. (2009) conducted a study with 34 participants in the intervention group and 37 in the control group, reporting no link between prenatal exercise and preterm birth. A meta-analysis by Du (2018) reviewed six randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 737 participants and found no significant difference in the risk of preterm birth among overweight or obese pregnant women who engaged in physical activity interventions compared to those who did not. However, the evidence was rated as very low quality due to serious imprecision and risk of bias. Two studies reported no cases of birth weight below 2500 grams, and their results were not included in the pooled analysis. Additionally, two studies provided data on different subgroups of women but were counted only once in the analysis. Some studies faced serious risks of bias, including high performance and attrition bias, as well as reporting bias. For example, one study included women who smoked during pregnancy, which could have influenced birth weight outcomes. Regarding miscarriage, Ussher (2015) found no effect of prenatal exercise on miscarriage odds after adjusting for recruitment center. However, Madsen (2007) observed a progressive increase in miscarriage odds with higher exercise volumes in a cohort of 92,671 women. Secondary analyses by Nilsson (2014), which included only women interviewed about exercise habits before miscarriage, showed no significant association. Zhang (2011) reported a protective dose-response effect of exercise on miscarriage after adjusting for confounding factors, while Maconochie (2007) found no association between exercise levels and miscarriage odds. For stillbirth, Ussher (2015) and Magnus (2008) found no significant effect of prenatal exercise on stillbirth odds. Dumith (2012) also reported no association between exercise and stillbirth after adjusting for confounding factors. Xu (2014) observed a protective effect of exercising at least 30 minutes twice a week compared to no exercise, but the evidence was rated as very low quality due to serious bias and imprecision. In terms of delivery complications, one systematic review addressed the relationship between physical activity and cesarean delivery risk. Kariminia et al. (2004) found similar cesarean section rates between walking and pelvic rocking exercise groups. Du (2018) reviewed 10 RCTs involving 982 participants and found no significant difference in cesarean delivery incidence among overweight or obese pregnant women engaging in physical activity interventions. Banerjee et al. (2013) reported a protective effect of abdominal exercises on diastasis recti postpartum compared to routine antenatal exercises. Overall, the evidence on prenatal exercise and its effects on pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, and delivery complications, is mixed and often limited by serious risks of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify these associations.
